name: National mysticism
summary: National mysticism treats the nation as a spiritually meaningful community with an enduring identity or transcendent mission. Scholarship uses the description across different national and religious settings; the common conception of nationhood leaves most detailed political institutions and policies unspecified.
scope: The broad descriptive family of nationalisms assigning spiritual significance to the national community: Cocău discusses organic national unity and a mystical national soul; Costea Dorle explicitly identifies national mysticism in Vasile Marin’s spiritual nationalism; Lutz identifies it in Gamsakhurdia’s cosmic account of national mission (s5–s7). These sources do not define the family as the combined programmes of Fichte, the Völkisch movement and the Romanian Legion, as the earlier Wikipedia-led scope did. Particular thinkers and movements establish association and illustrate the category, but their unrelated policies are not inherited as family tenets. No specific state or ruling-party doctrine is the record of this family as a whole. Söderman’s Swedish case (s8, pp. 307–308) likewise names national mysticism through an inherited national soul; its monarchism does not define the whole family.

sources.title: Ideologists and Doctrinaires of Inter-War Right-Wing Ideology
sources.author: Alina Costea Dorle
sources.usedFor: Pages 1725–1726 explicitly describe Vasile Marin’s national mysticism as spiritual transformation, religious commitment and national permanence. Its particular constitutional and economic proposals are not inherited by the whole family.

sources.title: Nationalism in the interwar period
sources.author: Andreea Cocău
sources.usedFor: Pages 12–16 discuss organic and mystical conceptions of the nation, a collective soul, historical community and national culture, and warn about rigid typologies.

sources.title: Spiritual Science and Sacred Tradition: The Esoteric Sources of Zviad Gamsakhurdia’s Worldview – Part I
sources.author: Alexander John Paul Lutz
sources.usedFor: Defines national mysticism in terms of a cosmic national identity and spiritual mission in a Georgian case; documents the descriptive term outside the old audit’s selected movements, without transferring the case’s policy positions.

sources.title: Dismantling Monarchy: The Swedish Experience
sources.author: Erik Söderman
sources.usedFor: Pages 307–308 identify Swedish national mysticism through a national soul and spirit inherited across generations; a further constitutional case, not a family-wide endorsement of Kjellén’s monarchism.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Cocău’s account of organic national mysticism centres shared culture, inherited traditions and collective identity; this supports preserving national culture without importing Fichte’s specific education programme.

sacred-nation.rationale: The defining accounts describe national community as a spiritual whole extending across generations: Cocău discusses its mystical soul, and Söderman identifies national mysticism through an inherited national soul and accumulated spiritual culture.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The defining accounts present spiritual national identity and human spiritual transformation as part of political life, rather than reducing politics to material interests.

notes: Later pass, 2026-11-08: checked every existing answer and every current statement, including candidates. The old audit had 282 known answers, often from Wikipedia about the Iron Guard or Völkisch movement, and many zero answers whose rationales admitted silence. Its two old missing statements were already marked addedAs and are not new gaps. New defining scholarship supports the spiritual conception of national community; it does not turn those movements’ programmes into the family’s own policy record. Each changed known answer preserves the committed version and the reason for revision in reviewHistory. Existing nulls retain nulledFrom provenance but lose obsolete citations as required by the validator. Reviewed original Fichte full text by theme as an earlier source, but did not treat all his political views as family tenets. Searched economy (healthcare, property, labour, markets), government (democracy, elections, constitutional authority), world (war, alliances, international authority), ecology (nature, land, environment), technology, liberty, society, culture and political means. Searched local reference, Gutenberg and Marxists texts for the name and close variants: no defining family treatment was found; Trotsky’s passing criticism in the Saar article is not evidence of this subject’s views. The parliamentary and broadcast corpora do not supply this family’s defining sources. Refused or unavailable leads: Concordia article 2908 and CEU Biliuta thesis returned 403; the MDPI article returned 429, and the publisher’s reprint download returned 403; Oxford’s Garb chapter could not be retrieved; JSTOR supplied a challenge rather than full text. GitHub searches for blocked texts yielded no usable mirror. No inaccessible text or third-party book upload was used as evidence. The family remains thin on policy and uncertainty exclusion is accepted rather than filling it from related movements. After the uncertainty failure named all 15 lines, searched specifically for family-wide positions on pluralism, class relations, regulation, church-state institutions, ethnicity, centralism, monarchy, national interests, gender, alliances, regional autonomy, revolution and territory. Söderman’s additional Swedish study documents another instance and strengthens the generational spiritual conception; its particular constitutional preference supplies no family-wide answer. Final uncertainty: all 15 lines remain unreached and the mean bar is infinite.
